keyword: what kills ticks on dogs instantly
metaTitle: What Kills Ticks on Dogs Instantly? Nothing Safe
metaDescription: Nothing safe kills an attached tick on a dog instantly. Tweezers remove it on the spot, and two tick chew labels report results at 48 or 72 hours.
h1: What Kills Ticks on Dogs Instantly? The Honest Answer and the Fastest Fix
dek: No product is shown to safely kill an attached tick on a dog instantly. Here is the removal method that works on the spot, how fast two tick chews act by their own labels, FDA's caution on the class, and the home remedies to skip.
excerpt: No safe product kills a tick on a dog instantly. Pull it with fine-tipped tweezers, then see how fast tick chews work by their labels and which home remedies to avoid.

quickAnswer.lead: **Nothing that is safe to use on a dog kills an attached tick instantly.** The fastest fix is to pull the tick out with fine-tipped tweezers, following [CDC's tick removal steps](https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/after-a-tick-bite/index.html), then drop it in alcohol or wrap it tightly in tape. Prescription tick chews work over hours to days: the NexGard and Bravecto labels report tick results at 48 or 72 hours after a tick gets on the dog.
bullets: Against blacklegged ticks, the NexGard label reports more than 94% effectiveness 48 hours after infestation and the Bravecto label reports at least 93%.
The fastest tick figure on either label is a European laboratory study in which Bravecto cut live *Ixodes ricinus* ticks by more than 98% within 12 hours.
Cornell's canine health center says fipronil spot-ons do not kill a tick until it has been attached for 24 hours.
CDC says not to use petroleum jelly, heat, nail polish or other substances to make an attached tick let go.
FDA considers isoxazoline chews safe and effective but has alerted owners to muscle tremors, ataxia and seizures in some dogs and cats.
In 443 poison-center cases of concentrated tea tree oil exposure in dogs and cats, signs developed within 2 to 12 hours.

body.text: What kills ticks on dogs instantly?

Nothing that is safe to put on a dog kills an attached tick instantly. The fastest fix is mechanical: pull the tick out with fine-tipped tweezers, which gets it off the dog on the spot, and dispose of the tick afterward. Every tick product covered by the sources for this page works more slowly than that.

That answer is a statement about the evidence. None of those sources, which are two FDA-approved product labels, FDA, CDC, Cornell's canine health center and a veterinary poisoning study, reports an instant kill. Two prescription chews, NexGard and Bravecto, report their tick results on the label at 48 or 72 hours after a tick gets on the dog, and the home remedies that promise a quicker kill put a substance or heat on an attached tick, which [CDC's instructions for removing a tick](https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/after-a-tick-bite/index.html) say not to do.

body.text: Speed matters because a feeding tick can pass an infection to the dog, and how long that takes depends on the pathogen. The transmission windows that veterinary guidelines give, which run from a few hours to a day or two, are set out in [the guide to ticks on dogs](/blog/ticks-on-dogs). That is the argument for pulling a tick the moment you find it and not waiting for a product to work. Killing ticks on the dog is also only one layer of protection, and [the full tick control guide for a home and yard](/blog/ultimate-tick-control-guide-ontario) covers the others.
How do you get a tick off a dog right now?

Grip the tick with clean, fine-tipped tweezers as close to the dog's skin as you can and pull it straight out with steady, even pressure. That is CDC's method, and CDC says to remove an attached tick as soon as possible. The agency wrote the steps for a tick on a person, and its page does not mention pets. The veterinary guidelines cited in the dog tick guide linked above describe the same technique for pets.

items: Part the fur so you can see the point where the tick meets the skin.
Grasp the tick with clean, fine-tipped tweezers as close to the skin's surface as possible. If you have no fine-tipped pair, CDC says regular tweezers or your fingers will do.
Pull away from the skin with steady, even pressure. Do not twist or jerk the tick.
If the mouthparts break off and will not come out easily with the tweezers, leave them alone. CDC says the body pushes them out as the skin heals.
Get rid of the live tick in one of the four ways CDC lists: place it in a sealed container, wrap it tightly in tape, flush it down the toilet or put it in alcohol. Do not crush it with your fingers.
Wash the bite area and your hands thoroughly with soap and water, the first of the cleaning options CDC lists. The others are rubbing alcohol and hand sanitizer.

body.text: Fine-tipped tweezers are the tool CDC names, and the agency notes that there are several tick removal devices on the market but that a plain set of tweezers works very well. Hook and key-style removers are covered in [a guide to tick removal tools and other tick gear](/pest-product-guides/tick-gear), and there is [a longer walkthrough of removing a tick from a dog](/blog/how-to-remove-tick-from-dog-ontario) if you want more detail. If part of the tick stays behind, read [what to do when a tick's head is stuck in the skin](/blog/tick-head-stuck-in-skin) before you start digging.
How fast do tick chews for dogs kill ticks?

The two labels checked for this page report tick kill at 48 or 72 hours after a tick gets on the dog, not in minutes. These chews belong to the isoxazoline class. [FDA's list of approved isoxazoline products](https://www.fda.gov/animal-veterinary/animal-health-literacy/fact-sheet-pet-owners-and-veterinarians-about-potential-adverse-events-associated-isoxazoline-flea) includes NexGard (afoxolaner), Bravecto (fluralaner), Simparica (sarolaner) and Credelio (lotilaner) tablets for dogs, along with a one-month Bravecto tablet and combination versions of NexGard and Simparica. [Cornell's Riney Canine Health Center](https://www.vet.cornell.edu/departments-centers-and-institutes/riney-canine-health-center/canine-health-topics/flea-and-tick-prevention) says the isoxazoline chewables do not prevent a tick from attaching but have a relatively fast tick kill time.

The figures below come from the Effectiveness sections of two FDA-approved labels as published on DailyMed, the National Library of Medicine's label database: [the NexGard label](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=e10f7434-d00c-44de-af79-7b0886b2e948) and [the Bravecto chew label](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=1fcbf232-cfd4-481e-ba9b-6251b7b468d7).

body.caption: Percent effectiveness in laboratory studies at the stated number of hours after infestation, as reported on each label. NexGard figures held for 30 or 31 days and Bravecto figures for 12 weeks unless noted. The studies were separate, so this is not a head-to-head comparison.

body.text: Read the table as a set of checkpoints. Each figure is the result at a fixed time after infestation in a laboratory study, and neither label states how soon the first tick dies. The species also matters. Both labels report lone star tick results at 72 hours, and the Bravecto label says the product failed to stay at 90% or better against that tick beyond 8 weeks. Its dosing section says the chew may be given every 8 weeks, in place of every 12, where lone star ticks are a potential exposure.

If you are not sure which tick you are looking at, [the identification guide to the common US ticks](/blog/what-do-ticks-look-like) describes the markings of five of the six species in the table. It does not cover the Asian longhorned tick.

The quickest numbers on these labels are for fleas. The NexGard label says the product began to kill fleas 4 hours after the first dose and was more than 99% effective at 8 hours, and the Bravecto label says it began to kill fleas within 2 hours. When you see a fast figure quoted for one of these products, check which parasite it refers to.

body.text: What is the fastest tick figure on either label?

More than 98% within 12 hours, on the Bravecto label, with a caveat. The label attributes that result to a European laboratory study in which the product reduced the number of live *Ixodes ricinus* ticks on dogs, and that species is not among the ticks in the label's indications. For the ticks the label does list, the stated results are at 48 and 72 hours.
Does killing the tick prevent Lyme disease?

The NexGard label carries a claim for it, limited to one bacterium and one tick. Its indications include preventing *Borrelia burgdorferi* infections as a direct result of killing *Ixodes scapularis* vector ticks, and the label cites two laboratory studies in which dogs were infested with those ticks 28 days after treatment. *Borrelia burgdorferi* is the bacterium behind Lyme disease, and the blacklegged tick is one of [the two US tick species that carry Lyme disease](/blog/ticks-that-carry-lyme-disease). The indications section of the Bravecto chew label does not include that claim. The NexGard indication says nothing about other tick-borne infections, and a label claim describes study results. It is not a promise for any one dog.
Does a chew work on a tick that is already attached?

The labels point that way, but neither reports it directly. Both carry an indication for the treatment and control of tick infestations, and treating an infestation implies acting on ticks that are already on the dog. Their Effectiveness sections, though, give results by hours after infestation and do not single out ticks that were attached before the dose. Either way the timescale is hours to days, so pull any tick you can see or feel and leave the ones you miss to the product.
Who can use these products?

Both are prescription drugs: each label carries the federal caution that restricts the drug to use by or on the order of a licensed veterinarian. NexGard is labeled for dogs and puppies 8 weeks of age and older that weigh 4 pounds or more, and it is given once a month, with or without food. Bravecto chews are labeled for dogs and puppies 6 months of age and older that weigh 4.4 pounds or more, and the label says to give them with food. Cornell lists Simparica and Credelio as monthly chews in the same class. Their labels were not reviewed for this page, so read them for their own tick results and their age and weight limits. Both labels reviewed here set the dose by the dog's body weight.
Do spot-on treatments and tick collars work faster than chews?

The sources for this page do not show a faster kill. What some of these products offer is action before the bite, which is a different thing. Cornell sorts the common products that are not swallowed this way:

items: **Spot-ons containing permethrin (K9 Advantix II, Vectra 3D).** These are applied monthly, and Cornell says they repel ticks and prevent attachment.

**Collars (Seresto).** Cornell says the collar repels fleas and ticks and can even prevent ticks from attaching, provided it is fitted tightly enough to touch the skin, and it lists the collar as lasting 8 months.

**Spot-ons containing fipronil (Frontline).** These are applied monthly. Cornell says they do not repel ticks or prevent attachment, so you may still see ticks crawling on the dog, and that fipronil does not kill a tick until it has been attached for 24 hours.

body.text: Cornell's page gives no kill time for the permethrin products or the collar, so the label of the exact product is the place to look for one. It does give two handling points: most topical products should be left to dry for two days before the dog is bathed or goes swimming, and a collar that is regularly submerged may not last as long. Cornell also says flea and tick preventives are generally very well tolerated and have a wide margin of safety, while noting that side effects are possible with any medication. The dog tick guide compares [how each type of tick preventive for dogs works](/blog/ticks-on-dogs) and takes up the year-round and vaccine questions.

body.title: Dog products and cats
body.text: Cornell notes that many products that are safe for dogs are not appropriate for cats and names K9 Advantix II as one. Use a tick product only on the species its label names, and ask a veterinarian before treating a dog that lives with a cat.
What has the FDA said about isoxazoline flea and tick products?

FDA says it considers the isoxazoline class safe and effective for dogs and cats, and it has also alerted owners and veterinarians that these drugs have been associated with neurologic adverse reactions. [The agency's fact sheet on isoxazoline flea and tick products](https://www.fda.gov/animal-veterinary/animal-health-literacy/fact-sheet-pet-owners-and-veterinarians-about-potential-adverse-events-associated-isoxazoline-flea), with content current as of August 8, 2023, names the reactions: muscle tremors, ataxia (loss of coordination) and seizures in some dogs and cats.

items: **Most animals are not affected.** FDA says most dogs and cats have not had neurologic adverse reactions.
**A clean history does not rule it out.** FDA says seizures may occur in animals with no prior history of them.

**Which dog products are covered.** FDA's list includes Bravecto and Bravecto 1-Month (fluralaner), Credelio (lotilaner), NexGard (afoxolaner), NexGard Plus (afoxolaner with moxidectin and pyrantel), Simparica (sarolaner) and Simparica Trio (sarolaner with moxidectin and pyrantel), along with Bravecto topical solution. It also lists products for cats.
**What FDA asks owners to do.** Review the pet's medical history with a veterinarian and decide together whether a product in the class is appropriate.
**Monitoring continues.** FDA says it continues to monitor adverse drug event reports for these products.

body.text: The same warning is printed on the products. The Precautions sections of the NexGard and Bravecto labels both state that the isoxazoline class has been associated with neurologic adverse reactions including tremors, ataxia and seizures, that seizures have been reported in dogs with no history of them, and that the drug should be used with caution in dogs with a history of seizures or neurologic disorders. Cornell describes seizures with these chewables as a rare occurrence and tells owners of a dog with a seizure history to consult a veterinarian before using one. In the field studies reported on both labels, the most frequently reported adverse reaction was vomiting.

If a dog trembles, staggers or has a seizure after a dose, FDA's instruction is to consult your veterinarian first. The reaction can then be reported to the manufacturer or directly to FDA. The fact sheet does not tell owners to avoid the class. It tells them to make the choice with a veterinarian who knows the dog's history.
What should you never use to kill a tick on a dog?

Do not put anything on an attached tick to kill it or to make it let go. CDC says not to use petroleum jelly, heat, nail polish or other substances to try to make a tick detach, because doing so may agitate the tick and force infected fluid from the tick into the skin. CDC names those three things and then adds other substances. Alcohol, essential oils and dish soap are not named one by one, and the table below reads them as falling under that last phrase.

body.caption: CDC's removal guidance is written for ticks on people. None of the veterinary sources used here gives a different rule for dogs.

body.text: Rubbing alcohol: after removal, not before

Alcohol has a job once the tick is off the dog. CDC lists putting a live tick in alcohol as one of four ways to dispose of it, and lists rubbing alcohol as one option for cleaning the bite area and your hands. The page does not say how long a tick takes to die in alcohol. Dabbing or pouring alcohol onto a tick that is still attached is a different act, and it falls under the substances CDC says not to use.
Essential oils and tea tree oil

Concentrated tea tree oil has a documented record of poisoning dogs. [A study in the Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24344857/) reviewed 443 cases of concentrated tea tree oil toxicosis recorded by the ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center from January 2002 to December 2012, in 337 dogs and 106 cats. In 395 of the 443 cases (89%), the 100% oil had been used intentionally, and the amounts ranged from 0.1 to 85 mL. Half of the exposures were on the skin only, and another 30% were on the skin and by mouth.

Signs developed within 2 to 12 hours and lasted up to 72 hours. The most common were increased salivation or drooling, lethargy or other signs of central nervous system depression, paresis (weakness or partial paralysis), ataxia and tremors. The authors concluded that intentional or accidental use of 100% tea tree oil in dogs or cats caused serious signs within hours of exposure.

Whether plant-oil sprays kill ticks at all is a separate question, and the short answer is that results vary widely from one product to the next. The guide to [what kills ticks, and what does not](/blog/what-kills-ticks) goes through a CDC-published review of those products, and a wider look at the category is in [which natural pest control methods hold up](/blog/natural-pest-control).
Dish soap

None of the sources used for this page supports dish soap as a tick killer. CDC, FDA's fact sheet, Cornell and the two product labels do not mention it as a tick treatment, and a soapy cotton ball held on an attached tick is the kind of substance-on-the-tick method CDC warns against. A bath has a second cost if the dog wears a spot-on product, because Cornell says most topical products should be left to dry for two days before bathing or swimming. Tweezers are quicker, and they do not depend on the tick letting go.

body.title: Only products labeled for dogs
body.text: Do not improvise with a product made for something else, such as a clothing treatment, a yard spray or another animal's medication. Use a tick product only as its label directs, on the species and weight range it names, and ask a veterinarian before combining two products.
Why is there still a tick on a dog that takes a preventive?

Because several kinds of preventive kill ticks only after they arrive, and the NexGard and Bravecto labels measure that kill 48 or 72 hours after infestation. Cornell says isoxazoline chewables do not prevent attachment, and that with a fipronil spot-on you may still see ticks crawling on the dog. A live or attached tick on a treated dog is therefore not proof that the product failed. It is a reason to keep running your hands over the dog after time outdoors and to pull what you find.
What kills ticks in the yard before they reach the dog?

A yard pesticide labeled for ticks can reduce the number of ticks in the areas it is applied to, and habitat work makes a yard less inviting to them, but neither replaces protection on the dog. CDC's tick prevention guidance, cited in the yard guide linked below, says not to rely on spraying to reduce the risk of infection. Cornell's description of the problem is the place to start: dogs get ticks in places where ticks live, such as tall grass and wooded areas, where the ticks wait to attach to a passing animal.

items: **Habitat.** Mow often, remove leaf litter, and clear tall grass and brush at the lawn edge. CDC also says to keep play equipment, decks and patios away from yard edges and trees, and the same logic applies to a dog run. CDC's full yard checklist, which includes a 3-foot-wide border of wood chips or gravel between lawn and woods, is set out in the guide to [what kills ticks in a yard](/blog/what-kills-ticks).

**Targeted treatment.** The same guide covers sprays and granules labeled for ticks, tick tubes and rodent bait boxes, along with a four-year New York trial that tracked tick-borne disease in pets as well as in people. Any yard product has to be used exactly as its label directs, including how long to keep pets off treated areas.
**Animals that eat ticks.** Backyard poultry gets more credit than the evidence supports, as the guide to [whether chickens eat enough ticks to matter](/blog/do-chickens-eat-ticks) explains.
**Season.** Cornell says ticks can be active at 40°F, which is not unusual in winter in many parts of the US, and calls year-round prevention the best practice.

body.text: The habitat work is laid out step by step in [a separate guide to keeping ticks out of a yard](/blog/how-to-keep-ticks-out-of-yard-ontario).
When should you call the veterinarian?

Call before you start a tick product, and call promptly if something looks wrong after a dose or after a bite. This page reports what labels and agencies say. It cannot tell you which product suits your dog.

items: **Before choosing a product.** FDA advises reviewing the dog's medical history with a veterinarian to decide whether an isoxazoline is appropriate, and Cornell says to consult a veterinarian first if the dog has a history of seizures or seizure disorders.

**After a dose.** Tremors, stumbling or a seizure call for the veterinarian first, by FDA's instruction. Cornell also lists anxiousness, itchiness, vomiting or diarrhea, and redness or irritation of the skin as possible side effects of preventives.

**Ticks you cannot deal with.** That includes more ticks than you can pull one at a time, a tick on an eyelid or deep in an ear, and a cluster of tiny larvae, described in the guide to [seed ticks, the larvae that arrive by the dozen](/blog/seed-ticks).

**After a bite.** If the dog seems unwell in the days and weeks that follow, check it against [the symptoms that can follow a tick bite on a dog](/blog/tick-bite-on-dog-symptoms) and tell the veterinarian when and where the tick was found.

faqs.question: Does rubbing alcohol kill ticks on dogs?
faqs.answer: Use alcohol only after the tick is off the dog. CDC lists putting a live tick in alcohol as one of four ways to dispose of it, along with sealing it in a container, wrapping it tightly in tape and flushing it down the toilet, and it lists rubbing alcohol as one option for cleaning the bite area afterward. Pouring or dabbing alcohol on a tick that is still attached is a different matter. CDC says not to use petroleum jelly, heat, nail polish or other substances to make a tick detach, because that may agitate the tick and force infected fluid into the skin.

faqs.question: Does Dawn dish soap kill ticks on dogs?
faqs.answer: None of the sources used for this page supports dish soap as a way to kill or remove a tick on a dog. CDC's removal guidance says not to put substances on an attached tick to make it let go, and a soapy cotton ball is one more substance. There is also a practical cost if the dog wears a spot-on product: Cornell's Riney Canine Health Center says most topical preventives should be left to dry for two days before bathing or swimming. Pulling the tick with fine-tipped tweezers is quicker, and it is the method CDC describes.

faqs.question: Which kills ticks faster, NexGard or Bravecto?
faqs.answer: Their labels do not settle it, because the figures come from separate studies. For blacklegged, American dog and brown dog ticks, both labels report results 48 hours after infestation: more than 93 to more than 97 percent for NexGard, depending on the species, and at least 93 percent for Bravecto. Both report lone star tick results at 72 hours. The Bravecto label also cites a European laboratory study in which live Ixodes ricinus ticks fell by more than 98 percent within 12 hours, but that species is not among the ticks in the label's indications. A veterinarian can weigh dosing interval, local tick species and the dog's history.

faqs.question: Can I give an isoxazoline chew to a dog that has had seizures?
faqs.answer: That is a decision to make with your veterinarian before the first dose. FDA says products in the isoxazoline class have been associated with muscle tremors, ataxia and seizures in some dogs and cats, and advises reviewing the pet's medical history with a veterinarian to decide whether a product in the class is appropriate. The NexGard and Bravecto labels both say to use the drug with caution in dogs with a history of seizures or neurologic disorders. FDA also notes that seizures may occur in animals with no prior history, which is a reason to watch any dog after a dose.

faqs.question: Can I use my dog's tick product on my cat?
faqs.answer: Not unless the label names cats. Cornell's Riney Canine Health Center notes that many products that are safe for dogs are not appropriate for cats and gives K9 Advantix II as an example. FDA's list of approved isoxazoline products shows that cats have their own versions, among them Bravecto Plus, NexGard Combo and Revolution Plus, which are topical solutions and are separate products from the dog chews. Ask a veterinarian which product suits a cat, and follow any instruction on a dog product's label about keeping treated dogs and cats apart.

faqs.question: Is tea tree oil safe to put on a tick on a dog?
faqs.answer: No. A study in the Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association reviewed 443 cases of concentrated tea tree oil toxicosis recorded by the ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center from 2002 to 2012, involving 337 dogs and 106 cats. In 89 percent of cases the 100 percent oil had been used intentionally, in amounts from 0.1 to 85 mL. Signs such as drooling, lethargy, weakness, incoordination and tremors developed within 2 to 12 hours and lasted up to 72 hours. Separately, CDC advises against putting any substance on an attached tick to make it detach.
